image.alt: Façade of angular sculpted figures beneath tall pointed spires
image.credit: Photo: Michielverbeek · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Begun in 1882 to a conventional Gothic Revival design, the expiatory church passed in 1883 to Gaudí, who reshaped it into a vast, forest-like basilica and worked on it until his death in 1926. Construction continues, funded by donations; in 2026 its central Tower of Jesus Christ reached 172.5 metres, making it the world's tallest church.
keyFeatures: Branching, tree-like columns
Three façades: Nativity, Passion and Glory
Towers for the apostles, the evangelists, Mary and Jesus
Geometry of hyperboloids and helicoids
funFacts: Its first architect, Francisco de Paula del Villar, resigned in 1883.
Pope Benedict XVI consecrated it as a basilica on 7 November 2010.
The central tower was blessed on 10 June 2026, a hundred years after Gaudí's death.

architects.name: Victor Horta
architects.bio: Born in Ghent, Horta designed a series of Brussels town houses in the 1890s that made him the pioneer of Art Nouveau architecture, with open plans, exposed iron and whiplash ornament. Four of them, including the Hôtel Tassel and his own house, form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

image.alt: Curved bay window with slender iron columns and flowing iron railings
image.credit: Photo: FrDr · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: A bow window framed in slender iron columns.

hints.text: It was built for a scientist and university professor, and is counted among the very first buildings of its style.

image.alt: Narrow stone town-house front with a projecting bow window of iron and glass
image.credit: Photo: Kat_hly.1608 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Designed by Victor Horta for the scientist and professor Émile Tassel and built in 1892–93, this Brussels town house is considered one of the first Art Nouveau buildings. Instead of the usual row of dark rooms, Horta arranged the house around a central stair hall, and let exposed iron and whiplash ornament flow through it.
keyFeatures: Central stair hall linking the different levels
Exposed iron columns, inside and on the façade
Whiplash ornament in iron, mosaic and paint
Projecting bow window
funFacts: It strongly influenced the French Art Nouveau architect Hector Guimard.
With three other Horta town houses, it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.

name: Glasgow School of Art
aliases: Glasgow School of Art Mackintosh Building

architects.name: Charles Rennie Mackintosh
architects.bio: Glasgow architect, designer and watercolourist and the leading figure of the Glasgow Style. Working with the firm Honeyman & Keppie, he won the 1896 competition for the School of Art; late in life he gave up architecture to paint watercolours in France.

architects.name: Margaret Macdonald Mackintosh
architects.bio: Artist and designer, one of 'The Four' of the Glasgow Style, and Charles Rennie Mackintosh's wife and collaborator.

image.alt: Tall sandstone wall with deep-set windows and a projecting stone bay
image.credit: Photo: Chilanga Cement · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: The west front rises sheer above a steep street.

hints.text: It was built in two phases, finished in 1899 and 1909.

image.alt: Stone façade with large studio windows, an off-centre entrance and curving iron railings
image.credit: Photo: Dave & Margie Hill / Kleerup · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Charles Rennie Mackintosh won the 1896 competition for the school's new building on Garnethill, which went up in two phases, completed in 1899 and 1909. Its huge north-facing studio windows, stark stone masses and inventive ironwork made it a landmark of early modern design. It was badly damaged by fire in 2014 and gutted by a second fire in 2018.
keyFeatures: Large north-facing studio windows
Asymmetrical stone façade with an off-centre entrance
Decorative wrought-iron brackets and railings
Library of timber columns and beams, lost in the 2014 fire
funFacts: Its library, one of Mackintosh's finest interiors, was destroyed in the 2014 fire.
Six recent Turner Prize winners studied at the school.

architects.name: Peter Behrens
architects.bio: A painter turned architect and designer, Behrens became AEG's artistic consultant in 1907 and shaped its buildings, products and graphics, an early corporate identity. Walter Gropius, Mies van der Rohe and Le Corbusier all worked in his office.

hints.text: A steel-framed hall about 100 metres long, with glass walls 15 metres tall, it brought restrained modern design to industrial building.
Its architect was also the company's artistic consultant, designing its products and its logo.

image.alt: Long industrial hall with tall glazed bays between steel columns, behind trees
image.credit: Photo: Oana Popa · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Built in 1909 in Berlin-Moabit for the electrical company AEG, Peter Behrens's turbine hall turned a factory shed into a 'temple of power'. Its steel frames are left exposed along the flanks, with huge glazed bays between them, while the massive gable recalls a classical pediment.
keyFeatures: 22 steel frames at 9-metre intervals
Huge windows angled slightly inwards
Exposed steel columns, bolts and joints
Polygonal gable echoing a temple front
funFacts: It was engineered by Karl Bernhard.
The hall was extended northwards in 1939 by Jacob Schallenberger and Paul Schmidt.
Walter Gropius, Mies van der Rohe and Le Corbusier all worked in Behrens's office.

architects.name: Frank Lloyd Wright
architects.bio: Over a career of some seventy years Wright developed an 'organic architecture' rooted in landscape, from the low, horizontal Prairie houses of the 1900s to Fallingwater and the Guggenheim Museum. Eight of his buildings form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

drawings.label: Longitudinal section and south elevation
drawings.alt: Long, low house in section and elevation, with wide overhanging roofs
drawings.credit: Historic American Buildings Survey (HABS ILL,16-CHIG,33-), measured drawing · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

image.alt: Brick terraces and planters under a deep overhanging roof
image.credit: Photo: erikccooper · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Brick terraces and flower urns beneath the eaves.

hints.text: Its roofs cantilever far beyond the walls, and its long horizontal lines echo the flat Midwestern prairie.

image.alt: Long, low brick house with deep overhanging roofs and bands of windows
image.credit: Photo: Carol M. Highsmith · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Completed in 1910 for the manufacturing executive Frederick C. Robie in Chicago's Hyde Park, this is often called the finest of Frank Lloyd Wright's Prairie houses. Its low brick walls, bands of art-glass windows and roofs cantilevered far beyond the walls stretch the house along its corner plot.
keyFeatures: Long, low horizontal lines
Roofs cantilevered far beyond the walls
Bands of art-glass windows
Terraces on several levels
funFacts: It helped popularise picture windows, deep eaves and attached garages in American houses.
It now belongs to the University of Chicago and is part of the UNESCO site 'The 20th-Century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright'.
It was one of the last buildings Wright designed at his Oak Park studio.

architects.name: Adolf Loos
architects.bio: Viennese architect and polemicist whose essay 'Ornament and Crime' attacked decoration as wasteful. His buildings pair plain exteriors with rich materials inside, and his Raumplan arranged rooms at different heights.

drawings.label: Ground floor plan
drawings.alt: Irregular corner-plot plan with a shop floor, columns and stairs
drawings.credit: FiliGelpi03 · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

drawings.label: Section
drawings.alt: Section through a multi-storey building: a shop below, plain apartment floors above
drawings.credit: FiliGelpi03 · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

image.alt: Marble-lined entrance passage with glass doors
image.credit: Photo: Thomas Ledl · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Rich marble lines the ground-floor entrance.

hints.text: Its plain upper floors caused such a scandal that the architect had to add flower boxes to the windows.

image.alt: Corner building with a green marble-clad base and plain white upper floors with window boxes
image.credit: Photo: Tilman2007 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Built for the tailors Goldman & Salatsch on Vienna's Michaelerplatz, opposite the imperial Hofburg, the building contrasts a base of green Cipollino marble with completely plain upper floors. In 1910 the bare façade caused a public scandal; construction resumed only after Loos agreed to add window boxes with flowers.
keyFeatures: Ground floor and mezzanine clad in green marble
Unornamented white upper storeys
Classical columns at the shop entrance
Window boxes added to quiet the critics
funFacts: Emperor Franz Joseph reportedly kept the Hofburg's curtains closed so he would not have to see it.
One newspaper called it a 'dung heap' before the flower boxes were added.

architects.name: Walter Gropius
architects.bio: After working for Peter Behrens, Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar in 1919 and moved it to Dessau in 1925. He emigrated in the 1930s and taught at Harvard, spreading modernist teaching in America.

architects.name: Adolf Meyer
architects.bio: Gropius's partner in his early practice and co-designer of the Fagus Factory; he later taught at the Bauhaus and became Frankfurt's city building director.

image.alt: Yellow brick factory buildings with a square tower and a tall chimney
image.credit: Photo: Ralf König · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Yellow brick buildings around a factory yard.

hints.text: Its owner made shoe lasts and wanted a building that broke with the past.

image.alt: Three-storey building whose glass walls wrap around a corner with no supporting pillar
image.credit: Photo: Ludvig14 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Built in 1911–13 for Carl Benscheidt's shoe-last company, the factory's main block wraps glass walls around its corners with no supporting pillar, turning the wall into a thin screen hung between recessed brick piers. It reversed the heavy corners of Behrens's AEG turbine hall, where both of its architects had worked.
keyFeatures: Glass curtain walls running the full height
Corners left free of supports
Brick piers set back behind the glass
Additions and interiors completed in 1925
funFacts: Gropius described the walls as 'mere screens stretched between the upright columns of the framework'.
It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011.
The factory still makes shoe lasts.

architects.name: Erich Mendelsohn
architects.bio: Mendelsohn sketched fluid, dynamic buildings while serving in the First World War; the Einstein Tower made his name, followed by department stores in Germany. He left in 1933, working in Britain, Palestine and the United States.

image.alt: Large telescope mirror mounted in a white instrument chamber
image.credit: Photo: Bautsch · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Inside, mirrors send sunlight down a shaft to the laboratory.

hints.text: It was built to test a famous scientist's theory of relativity by observing the Sun.

image.alt: Smooth, curving white tower topped by a small dome, among trees
image.credit: Photo: Muck · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Designed by Erich Mendelsohn and built in 1919–21 on the Telegraphenberg in Potsdam, this solar observatory houses a telescope built to test Albert Einstein's theory of relativity. Its flowing, sculptural form was imagined in concrete, but wartime shortages meant much of it was built in brick covered with stucco.
keyFeatures: Fluid, sculptural Expressionist form
Dome housing the coelostat at the top
Shaft sending light down to a basement laboratory
Brick and stucco shaped to look like poured concrete
funFacts: Einstein never worked there, but he supported its construction.
It is still a working solar observatory.
The young Richard Neutra was on Mendelsohn's staff during the project.

architects.name: Gerrit Rietveld
architects.bio: A cabinetmaker turned architect, Rietveld joined the De Stijl movement and designed the Red and Blue Chair before building this house with Truus Schröder. He went on to a long career in Utrecht.

image.alt: White and grey planes and balconies with thin red, yellow and blue lines
image.credit: Photo: FrDr · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Planes, lines and primary colours.

hints.text: Its upper floor can be one open space or divided into rooms with sliding and revolving panels.

image.alt: Small house of overlapping white and grey planes at the end of a brick terrace
image.credit: Photo: Luis Guillermo R. · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Built in 1924 for Truus Schröder-Schräder and her three children at the end of a brick terrace in Utrecht, the house is the purest built expression of De Stijl: free-floating planes, lines and primary colours. Its upper floor can be opened into one space or divided into rooms with sliding and revolving panels.
keyFeatures: Composition of independent planes and lines
Primary colours with white, grey and black
Flexible upper floor with sliding partitions
Corner windows that open to remove the corner entirely
funFacts: It included a garage, though Truus Schröder did not own a car.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.

architects.name: Walter Gropius
architects.bio: After working for Peter Behrens, Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar in 1919 and moved it to Dessau in 1925. He emigrated in the 1930s and taught at Harvard, spreading modernist teaching in America.

image.alt: White wing with bands of windows linked to a glass block across a lawn
image.credit: Photo: Spyrosdrakopoulos · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: White wings with bands of windows meet a glass block.

hints.text: Its wings for workshops, classrooms and student studios are linked by a two-storey bridge over a road.

image.alt: Workshop wing with a continuous glass curtain wall, beside a lower white wing
image.credit: Photo: Spyrosdrakopoulos · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Built in 1925–26 when the Bauhaus school moved from Weimar to Dessau, Gropius's building gives each function its own wing: a workshop block behind a glass curtain wall, a technical school, and a five-storey studio house for students, joined by a bridge over the road and a low wing with the hall and canteen.
keyFeatures: Glass curtain wall of the workshop wing
Pinwheel plan of separate wings
Two-storey bridge spanning a road
Studio house with small balconies
funFacts: The 28 studios in the five-storey Prellerhaus were living and working space for students and young masters.
Curtains needed for sun protection spoiled the intended transparency of the glass wall.
It has been part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996.

architects.name: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe
architects.bio: A former assistant of Peter Behrens, Mies reduced architecture to steel, glass and fine materials ('less is more'). Last director of the Bauhaus, he emigrated to Chicago, where he built the Illinois Institute of Technology campus and later the Seagram Building in New York.

architects.name: Lilly Reich
architects.bio: Designer and Mies's close collaborator in the late 1920s and 1930s, co-author of the pavilion and its furniture, and head of the Bauhaus weaving and interior workshops.

image.alt: Black-and-white view of a thin flat roof over a shallow pool and a travertine plinth
image.credit: Photo: Alexander.Hüls · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: A thin roof floats over a shallow pool.

hints.text: It was demolished less than a year after it opened, and rebuilt on the same site in 1986.

image.alt: Low pavilion of stone walls and glass under a flat roof, beside a pool
image.credit: Photo: Ashley Pomeroy at English Wikipedia · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Built as Germany's pavilion for the 1929 International Exposition in Barcelona, it held no exhibits: only the building itself, a sculpture by Georg Kolbe and furniture designed for it. Free-standing walls of marble, onyx and tinted glass divide a flowing space under a thin flat roof on slender steel columns.
keyFeatures: Thin flat roof on cruciform steel columns
Free-standing walls of marble, onyx and glass
Travertine plinth and reflecting pools
Open, flowing plan
funFacts: The Barcelona chair was designed for it and is still made today.
It was torn down in early 1930 and reconstructed in 1986.

architects.name: Konstantin Melnikov
architects.bio: One of the boldest Soviet avant-garde architects of the 1920s, Melnikov designed the USSR pavilion at the 1925 Paris exhibition and a series of workers' clubs in Moscow, before falling out of favour in the 1930s.

image.alt: White cylinder pierced by rows of hexagonal windows, among trees
image.credit: Photo: Mike1979 Russia · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: A white cylinder pierced by hexagonal windows.

hints.text: The architect built it in 1927–29 as a home and studio for himself and his family.

image.alt: Two interlocking white cylinders with a tall glazed front, behind a fence
image.credit: Photo: Александр Спиридонов · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Konstantin Melnikov built this house and studio for his family in a lane off the Arbat in central Moscow. It is made of two interlocking cylinders whose walls are pierced by rows of hexagonal windows, a rare private house in the Soviet capital.
keyFeatures: Two interlocking cylinders
Rows of hexagonal windows
Tall glazed front on the street side
Studio and living spaces in one home
funFacts: The design grew out of an unrealised competition project for the Zuev workers' club.
The construction estimate rose from about 25,000 to nearly 38,000 roubles.

architects.name: Isidore of Miletus
architects.bio: Greek geometer and engineer from Miletus, commissioned by Emperor Justinian I to design the new cathedral of Constantinople with Anthemius of Tralles.

architects.name: Anthemius of Tralles
architects.bio: Greek mathematician and engineer from Tralles in Asia Minor, co-designer of Hagia Sophia for Emperor Justinian I.

drawings.label: Ground plan
drawings.alt: Plan of a huge rectangular church with a central square crowned by a circle and half-domes at each end
drawings.credit: 19th-century engraving · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

drawings.label: Longitudinal section
drawings.alt: Section through a vast church with a shallow central dome on a ring of windows
drawings.credit: 19th-century engraving · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

image.alt: Vast interior under a golden dome ringed with windows, with large calligraphic roundels
image.credit: Photo: Kemal KOZBAEV · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: A dome ringed by windows seems to float over the nave.

hints.text: For nearly a thousand years it enclosed the largest interior space in the world.

image.alt: Domed building with minarets on a hill above a waterfront city
image.credit: Photo: Photograph by Mike Peel (www.mikepeel.net). · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Built for Emperor Justinian I between 532 and 537 and designed by the geometers Isidore of Miletus and Anthemius of Tralles, Hagia Sophia was the cathedral of Constantinople. Its vast dome, one of the first carried on pendentives, rests on a ring of windows. It became a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1935, and a mosque again in 2020.
keyFeatures: Central dome on pendentives
Ring of 40 windows at the base of the dome
Half-domes extending the central space
Minarets added after 1453
funFacts: It became the model for Ottoman mosques a thousand years later.
It was Turkey's most visited tourist attraction in 2019.

architects.name: Filippo Brunelleschi
architects.bio: Trained as a goldsmith, Brunelleschi is credited with rediscovering linear perspective and with founding Renaissance architecture through works such as the Foundling Hospital and San Lorenzo in Florence. His dome solved a problem that had defeated builders for decades.

drawings.label: Section of the dome (Cigoli, c. 1613)
drawings.alt: Hand-drawn section of a tall pointed dome with an inner and outer shell, surrounded by notes
drawings.credit: Lodovico Cardi (Cigoli), drawing, c. 1613 · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

image.alt: Gothic nave of tall pointed arches leading to a domed octagon
image.credit: Photo: Zde · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: The nave leads to a vast octagonal crossing.

hints.text: Its builder won a competition against the goldsmith Lorenzo Ghiberti.

image.alt: Huge red-tiled ribbed dome with a lantern above a city of terracotta roofs
image.credit: Photo: Nan Palmero · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: The cathedral of Florence was begun in 1296 to a design by Arnolfo di Cambio, but its huge octagonal crossing stood open for decades. Filippo Brunelleschi built the dome between 1420 and 1436 without the timber centring normally used, and it remains the largest masonry dome ever built.
keyFeatures: Octagonal dome of two shells
Eight white marble ribs over red tile
Built without full timber centring
Lantern crowning the dome
funFacts: Pope Eugene IV consecrated the cathedral on 25 March 1436.
Guillaume Dufay's motet Nuper rosarum flores was written for the consecration.
Brunelleschi and Ghiberti were appointed jointly, a rivalry that lasted for years.

name: Tempietto of San Pietro in Montorio

architects.name: Donato Bramante
architects.bio: Born near Urbino, Bramante worked in Milan before moving to Rome in 1499. The Tempietto launched the High Renaissance there, and in 1503 Pope Julius II charged him with rebuilding St Peter's Basilica.

drawings.label: Plan (Palladio, 1570)
drawings.alt: Circular plan: a ring of columns around a round cella with niches
drawings.credit: Andrea Palladio, woodcut, 1570 · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

drawings.label: Planned courtyard (Serlio)
drawings.alt: Plan of a small round temple at the centre of a colonnaded circular courtyard
drawings.credit: Sebastiano Serlio, woodcut · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

image.alt: Small round domed temple with a Doric colonnade inside a courtyard, at dusk
image.credit: Photo: Bradley  Weber · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: A tiny round temple in a cloister.

hints.text: It marks the spot where Saint Peter was traditionally believed to have been martyred.

image.alt: Round temple with a ring of columns and a dome, beside a bell tower
image.credit: Photo: JTSH26 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Commissioned around 1502 for the courtyard of San Pietro in Montorio on the Janiculum, Bramante's tiny round temple marks the traditional site of Saint Peter's martyrdom. Ringed by Doric columns and crowned by a dome, it applies ancient Roman proportions so rigorously that it is seen as the beginning of the High Renaissance in Rome.
keyFeatures: Circular plan with a peristyle of Doric columns
Hemispherical dome on a drum
Balustrade above the colonnade
Strict classical proportions at small scale
funFacts: Serlio's engraving shows that Bramante planned to set it in a circular colonnaded courtyard, never built.
It was commissioned by Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile, or possibly by Pope Julius II.

architects.name: Frank Lloyd Wright
architects.bio: Over a career of some seventy years Wright developed an 'organic architecture' rooted in landscape, from the low, horizontal Prairie houses of the 1900s to Fallingwater and the Guggenheim Museum. Eight of his buildings form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

drawings.label: Second floor plan
drawings.alt: House plan with terraces jutting out over a stream
drawings.credit: Arsenalbubs · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

image.alt: Cantilevered horizontal terraces among dense green woodland
image.credit: Photo: Carol M. Highsmith · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Terraces jut out among the trees.

hints.text: It was a weekend house for the owner of a Pittsburgh department store and his wife.

image.alt: House of stacked cantilevered terraces over a waterfall in a wood
image.credit: Photo: Bmzuckerman · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Frank Lloyd Wright designed this weekend house in 1934 for Edgar and Liliane Kaufmann, who owned a Pittsburgh department store, and built it directly over a waterfall on Bear Run. Reinforced-concrete terraces cantilever out from a stone core above the falls; the family moved in in 1937, and a guest wing followed in 1939.
keyFeatures: Cantilevered concrete terraces
Stone chimney core rising from the rock
Built over a waterfall
Bands of glass opening to the woods
funFacts: It has been open to visitors since 1963, run by the Western Pennsylvania Conservancy.
It is part of the UNESCO site 'The 20th-Century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright'.

architects.name: Robert Venturi
architects.bio: Philadelphia architect whose 1966 book Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture challenged modernist purity. With his partner Denise Scott Brown he became a central figure of postmodernism, and he received the Pritzker Prize in 1991.

image.alt: Back of a small house with a pitched roof and a chimney rising behind
image.credit: Photo: Smallbones · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: A pitched roof and an emphatic chimney.

hints.text: The architect designed it for his mother while writing a book attacking modernist orthodoxy.

image.alt: House front with a split gable and an applied arch over the door
image.credit: Photo: Carol M. Highsmith · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Robert Venturi built this house for his mother in Philadelphia's Chestnut Hill in 1962–64. With its broken gable, ornamental arch and big central chimney it deliberately reverses modernist rules, and it became one of the first landmarks of postmodern architecture.
keyFeatures: Split pediment on the long front
Non-structural applied arch
Central chimney and stair dominating the plan
Pitched roof instead of a flat one
funFacts: Vanna Venturi lived there until 1973 and liked to lecture visiting architects.
Its ideas appear in Venturi's 1966 book Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture.

name: Leça Swimming Pools
aliases: Tidal Pools of Leça da Palmeira
Piscinas de Marés de Leça da Palmeira

architects.name: Álvaro Siza
architects.bio: Born in Matosinhos, near Porto, Siza is known for restrained white and concrete buildings shaped closely to their sites. He received the Pritzker Prize in 1992.

image.alt: Narrow passages between raw concrete walls open to the sky
image.credit: Photo: Pedro Layant · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Raw concrete walls lead down to the sea.

hints.text: Its two pools are filled with fresh sea water and set among rocks on an Atlantic beach.

image.alt: Swimming pool set among rocks on the seashore
image.credit: Photo: Ricardo Saraiva de Almeida · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Designed and built between 1960 and 1973 by the young Álvaro Siza on the beach at Leça da Palmeira, near Porto, the pools use concrete walls to channel visitors from the road down to two sea-water pools set among the natural rocks.
keyFeatures: Two sea-water pools set among rocks
Raw concrete walls guiding the route to the sea
Changing rooms tucked below the road
Minimal intervention in the shoreline
funFacts: It is one of Siza's earliest works, after the nearby Boa Nova tea house.
A restoration from 2019 to 2021 cost €1.3 million, with Siza involved.

architects.name: Jørn Utzon
architects.bio: Utzon won the 1957 competition for the Opera House with a design that made his name, but resigned in 1966 amid disputes over cost and design. He received the Pritzker Prize in 2003.

architects.name: Peter Hall
architects.bio: Australian architect who led the team that completed the Opera House, including its interiors, after Utzon's resignation.

image.alt: Close-up of curved white shells covered in a fine chevron pattern of tiles
image.credit: Photo: Glinted framora · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: The shells are covered in over a million tiles.

hints.text: Its architect won an international competition of 233 entries in 1957, but left before it was finished.

image.alt: White sail-like shells on a podium by a harbour, with skyscrapers behind
image.credit: Photo: Bengt Nyman · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Jørn Utzon won the 1955–57 competition with a design of white concrete 'shells' rising from a monumental podium on Bennelong Point. After disputes over cost and design he resigned in 1966, and an Australian team led by Peter Hall completed the building, which Queen Elizabeth II opened on 20 October 1973.
keyFeatures: Roof 'shells' cut from a sphere of 75.2 m radius
1,056,006 glossy white and matte cream tiles
Monumental podium clad in pink granite
Glass walls closing the shells' open ends
funFacts: The shells are actually precast concrete panels on precast ribs, not shells in the structural sense.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007.
The competition drew 233 entries from 32 countries.
